analytic.title: Worst case response time analysis of sporadic graph tasks with fixed priority scheduling on a uniprocessor

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: This paper considers the problem of hard real-time fixed priority scheduling of sporadic graph tasks on a uniprocessor. We study feasibility conditions based on the computation of the worst case response times of the graph tasks. A sporadic graph task associated to an application is characterized by a set of subtasks under precedence constraints. We investigate the late deadline constraint. We extend already published papers established in the preemptive case to the non-preemptive case and to the hybrid case of an application composed of preemptive and non preemptive subtasks.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: A real time system can be composed of one or more real time applications running concurrently. We consider in this paper a real time application composed of a graph of subtasks. Among these subtasks, some could be preempted during their executions, while others cannot be interrupted once they have begun their executions even if a subtask arrives with higher priority during their execution (e.g. kernel tasks or network communication tasks).
In this paper, we study the problem of scheduling a set of sporadic graph tasks on a uniprocessor in a hard real time environ ment. This model is more formally defined in the next section.

We propose to establish a feasibility condition for fixed priority scheduling based on the computation of the worst case response time of the graph tasks. The fixed priority scheduling theory, known as the basic scheduling theory chosen by the practical Real Time System world, has been extensively studied in the last thirty years. The first theoretical treatment of periodic fixed priority scheduling for independent tasks was first studied in [1]. They proved the optimality of Rate Monotonic algorithm in the case of deadlines equal to the period in the preemptive context. This was developed by [4], [10] and [11] in a more general case.

The feasibility analysis for the independent task of preemptive scheduling based on the computation of the task's worst case response time was introduced by [8], while the non preemptive scheduling case was introduced by [2], [3] and [11]. The feasibility analysis for dependent tasks with preemptive scheduling was proposed by [6], [7], and it was developed by [9] in the case of re entrant graph. In this paper, we first recall classical concepts and notations in section 2. We describe the sporadic graph model and show how to transform a graph in a canonical chain, using the method proposed in [6]. The canonical chain is used to establish the response time of a graph task. We recall the feasibility conditions for preemptive graph task scheduling in section 3.2. In section 3.3, we propose new results for the feasibility of non preemptive graph scheduling. Section 3.4, is devoted to the study hybrid scheduling, considering the case of graphs having both preemptive and non preemptive subtasks. An example of hybrid graph feasibility analysis is proposed in section 4. Finally, we conclude.

div.head: Notations
div.p: In this paper, we consider a set τ ={τ 1 ,…,τ n } of n sporadic graph tasks. A Sporadic graph task τ i , is defined by: • G i : a graph of subtasks with precedence constraints,

• T i : the minimum inter arrival time, abusively called the period of the graph task • D i : the relative deadline of the graph task (a graph task released at time t must be executed by its absolute deadline t + D i ) By definition, G i (τ i )={τ i 1 ,…τ i ni } is the set of n i subtasks composing the graph G i . Notice that a subtask can be preemptive or not. A partial order is defined for the subtasks, the order specifying operation precedence constraints. τ i j < τ i k , means that τ i j must be completed before τ i k .

A subtask τ i j of a graph task τ i is defined by: • C i j : its execution duration • T i : the minimum inter arrival time or period (every subtask inherits the period of its graph task). • π i j : the fixed priority of subtask τ i j . the value 0 is the highest priority.
Furthermore, we assume that:

• Time is discrete (task arrivals occur and task executions begin and terminate at clock ticks; the parameters used are expressed as multiples of the clock tick); in [12], it is shown that there is no loss of generality with respect to feasibility results through restricting the schedules to being discrete, once the task parameters are assumed to be integers (multiples of the clock tick) i.e. a discrete schedule exists, if and only if a continuous schedule exists. • An idle time t is defined on a processor as a time, such that there are no subtasks released before time t pending at time t. An interval of successive idle times is called an idle period. • A busy period is defined as a time interval [a,b), such that there is no idle time in [a,b) (the processor is fully busy) and such that both a and b are idle times.

div.head: Graph to chain transformation
div.p: All the graphs can be transformed into a chain of subtasks, which are easier to analyse. The following rule can transform a graph G i of a task τ i into a chain:
1. Set chain to empty.

2. Consider all the subtasks in the graph having no predecessor. Select among those subtasks the highest priority subtask, insert it at the end of the current chain and remove it from the graph 3. Proceed to point 2 until the graph is empty
After the transformation, the subtasks are indexed by increasing order from τ i 1 to τ i ni . In the following sections, τ i j therefore represents the j th task in the chain.

[9] proved that this transformation would not change the schedulability problem. We now transform the chain into its canonical form w.r.t a subtask τ i j . This transformation is required for the response time computation (see section 3.2 to 3.4). This modification consists in changing the priority of a subtask τ i m 1 to the priority of τ i m if its priority is higher than τ i m , starting from m=j down to m=2. This allows obtaining a set of consecutive subtasks with equal or increasing priority from τ I 1 to τ i j . The priority of the subtasks after τ i j are left unchanged. The consecutive subtasks in the canonical chain with equal priority can be combined into a single subtask for the feasibility analysis. The execution duration of this single subtask is equal to the sum of execution duration of all the subtasks included. [6], [7] proved that the execution of a subtask τ i j and the execution duration of its canonical form τ i j ′ were the same. We now define the other notions for the computation of the worst case response time of a subtask τ i j in canonical chain obtained from the graph of task τ i .
• P i : the corresponding chain of graph G i .
• P i,j * : the canonical chain. • τ i j : the j th task in the chain P i .

• j i C , max : the longest execution duration of a subtask among those subtasks with lower priority than τ i j . • π i (j) : the lowest priority from the first subtask (τ i 1 ) in the canonical chain to the subtask studied (τ i j ). • π i j* : the fixed priority of subtask τ i j in its canonical chain.

The concept of a busy period is well known in queuing theory and was first introduced in real time scheduling by [5]. Here we need to modify this concept slightly.

In the following we only consider worst case busy periods. For a given subtask τ i j , we have for any integer k≥0: • τ i j (k): the k th activation of subtask τ i j in a given level τ i j busy period. • W i,j,k (t) : the k th instance workload of subtask τ i j . This is the amount of processing time of those subtasks with higher priority than τ i j whose release times are in the interval [0,t) for preemptive subtask and respectively [0,t] for non preemptive subtask.
• F i,j (k) : the finish time of the k th instance of subtask τ i j . • r i j : the worst case response time of any instance of subtask τ i j

The value 0 indicates the highest priority. Thus, if π i k > π i j then, subtask τ i k has lower priority than τ i j . In this example, we suppose that τ 1 5 is the subtask studied.

div.head: Real-Time Analysis
div.p: In this section we first recall already published papers for the feasibility analysis of the preemptive graph tasks. We then propose new results in the non preemptive case.

Finally, we extend the analysis to the hybrid case of both preemptive and non preemptive subtasks. The feasibility analysis is based on determining the worst case response time of subtasks of a graph. For that purpose, we first describe the general principles required to determine this worst case response time.

div.head: General principles
div.p: We describe a procedure for determining the worst case response time of a single subtask in a graph. The procedure used can be subsequently applied to all the subtasks in the graph. Thus we may get a sufficient feasibility condition based on the worst case response time of the last subtask of the graph.
This procedure includes 5 steps for a given graph task τ i and for a subtask τ i j .

1. Transform all the graphs into chains of subtasks and transform the chain of τ i into its canonical form w.r.t τ i j . 2. Regroup subtasks in segments according to π i (j). 3. For subtask τ i j , in the worst case level τ i j busy period, determine the maximum number of activations of τ i j . 4. Compute the worst case response time of subtask τ i j (k) for every activation in the τ i j busy period. Take the maximum value to obtain r i j . 5. Reiterate the principle until reaching the last subtask of the canonical chain of τ i and check that its response time is less than or equal to the Graph deadline Di.
We presented the principle to transform a graph into canonical chain in section 2.2. In the following section we describe how to regroup the subtasks of a canonical chain into segments

div.head: Grouping subtasks into segments
div.p: To simplify the computation of the worst case response time of the subtask studied, we regroup subtasks into two types of segments. We refer to a sequence of consecutive subtasks as a segment. An H segment comprises a sequence of consecutive subtasks which have a priority greater than or equal to π i j* . Notice that considering the equal priority subtask in H segment is a possibly pessimistic treatment. Similarly, an L segment includes only the subtasks which have priority strictly less than π i j* . Since an L segment is never able to preempt the chain studied, we only consider the interference of H segments on the subtask studied. [9] showed the different type of interferences of H segments. Interference of segments of the chain P j , j≠i, on P i,j * : We first consider the interference of the other chains. Note that an L segment has no effect on τ i j . There are two different effects of an H segment which is preceded or not by an L segment on τ i j • Blocking effect : When an H segment is preceded by an L segment, this H segment can not be executed unless the L segment ends its execution just before the beginning of the level τ i j busy period. [9] proved that among these H segments, only one can interfere in the busy period. We denote these segments H sb .
• Preemption effect: When an H segment does not have any L segment as predecessor, it can be activated several times during the busy period. We denote these segments H mp .
Interference of segments of the canonical chain itself: we now analyse P i,j * , the canonical chain studied.

• Blocking effect (H sb ): An H segment of chain P i preceded by an L segment can block the subtask studied once. • Preemption effect (H mp ): All the subtasks before the subtask studied in the chain should be considered as the H segment (include the subtask studied itself). This H segment can be active several times in the busy period of level τ i j . • Multiple blocking effect (H mb ): Given that our chain was re entrant, the segment H which is just following the subtask studied (if any) is also taken into account. Suppose that in the busy period of level τ i j , the canonical chain studied could be active several times, this H segment could block the execution of the current canonical chain studied. Suppose in the busy period of level τ i j , the chain could be active k times, then there are (k 1) blocking induced by this segment.

div.head: The non-preemptive case
div.p: In this section, we study the non preemptive case. In a non preemptive system, when a subtask begins processing, it cannot be interrupted until its execution duration is completed. Thus a subtask can possibly block another higher priority subtask if it is processed before the higher priority subtask. What is more, it should be remarked that in the non preemptive case, we compute the starting time of a subtask instead of the finish time, leading to a modification of the workload computation interval. The subtask's finish time is equal to its starting time plus its execution.

div.head: The hybrid case of preemptive and nonpreemptive scheduling
div.p: In this section, we propose a method of feasibility analysis for the hybrid case. The feasibility analysis follows the same procedure as preemptive or non preemptive case. As introduced in section 3, the response time of subtask τ i j only depends on the finish time of it predecessor and the effect of those H mp segments except subtask τ i 1 . Since an H mp segment is always composed of subtasks having higher priority than τ i j , there is no difference whether those higher priority subtasks are preemptive or not. For any preemptive subtask τ i j given, we compute its finish time and use the equation ( 5),( 6) to determine its worst case response time. If it is non preemptive, we compute its starting time and use the equation ( 8), (6) for determining its worst case response time. For subtask τ i 1 , whether it is preemptive or not, the blocking term always includes the effect of those non preemptive subtasks which have lower priority than it in the system. div.head: Conclusion
div.p: In this paper, we have studied the problem of scheduling the graph tasks with fixed priority scheduling. We have recalled existing feasibility conditions in the case of preemptive subtasks. We have then studied graph with non preemptive subtasks and hybrid case of preemptive and non preemptive subtasks. We have shown in an example how to use the feasibility conditions we have established in the hybrid case of both preemptive and non preemptive subtasks in a graph task.
